messages.subject: Today's SDM quiz
parts:
Dear all,

here is a quiz: why does imperfect detection bias estimates of the slopes of covariates in presence/absence SDMs, but not in abundance SDMs ? See attached.

First person who gives a convincing explanation gets a beer, a wine or a book, if we happen to meet 🙂

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
parts:
I would say it's because the contamination is one-sided with presence/absence data, which causes the effect size to be underestimated on average.  With abundance, the imperfect detection is an equal opportunity phenomenon so the relative comparisons still hold.  The stark difference in accuracy/precision also highlights how hungry the logistic regression is for data, and the greater relative value of counts over 0/1s.

I bet that even if you model p, the occupancy slopes will be slightly underestimated.

messages.author: bed9858844040a0b
messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
parts: I think it's because imperfect detection for presense/absence is imperfect detection of the species, which is related with abundance (the species is more detectable where it is more abundant). Because abundance is greater where occupancy is greater, imperfect detection declines with increasing abundance and increasing occupancy, resulting less of an upward correction of occupancy at the right side of the gradient. For abundance, imperfect detection is at the individual level and therefore not related with abundance and therefore even across the covariate gradient.

messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
parts:
Hello, very interesting behaviour :)
I think it goes more into the root of the distributions used. Using Poisson regression may bring more information to the model and and a more precise posterior distribution will be obtain. 
when you convert the data from count to 0/1 somehow you are loosing information, thus the estimates are more imprecise. 

I quickly generated several data sets where the outcome is a Poisson distributed and the mean parameter is modeled via a random covariate. Build two GLM models (Poisson and Bernoulli distributed). Poisson model uses data as generated, for the Bernoulli model transform data to 0/1 is used, and run some MCMC. Standard deviation of the posterior distributions for the estimate value of the covariate are smaller in when the data used is count.

messages.author: 074a030d0cd7e490
messages.subject: Re: Today's SDM quiz
parts: Daniel’s comment about one-sided contamination made me wonder what would happen if there were false positives that were not accounted for in the model.  The pattern that Marc showed in the original e-mail persists after changing the simOcc function to include some observation-level false positives (see fig). It makes sense that it does because false detections in sites that do not have the species must blur the relationship with the covariates. There are different sorts of two-sided contaminations.
